            Standard GRU interpolation is h_t = z_t⊙h_previous + (1−z_t)⊙candidate; its reset gate filters history inside the candidate computation ([Cho et al., 2014](https://arxiv.org/abs/1406.1078)). Algebraically, the proposed carry-gated update equals standard interpolation minus z_t⊙(1−r_t)⊙h_previous. For sigmoid gates, the coefficients sum to 1−z_t⊙(1−r_t) ≤ 1: the missing mass can be interpreted as interpolation toward zero. Thus it introduces coordinatewise carry attenuation and permits forgetting without a compensating increase in candidate weight. This does not guarantee a smaller total state norm, because the candidate may reinforce or cancel the carried state.

Adaptive forgetting is established prior work: LSTM forget gates explicitly attenuate stored state independently of writing ([Gers et al., 2000](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11032042/)). The proposed rule has effective forget coefficient f_t=z_t⊙r_t and write coefficient i_t=1−z_t, constrained by f_t+i_t≤1. Its distinction from standard GRU is gating the direct carry path; selective forgetting itself is not novel. The search did not establish whether this exact parameterization is new.

Holding gate and candidate dependencies fixed, the direct temporal Jacobian changes from diag(z_t) to diag(z_t⊙r_t); repeated carry-path gradients therefore acquire additional multiplicative attenuation. Long retention requires both gates near one. This is a mechanistic deduction, not a guarantee about the full Jacobian, which includes candidate and gate derivatives. Prior dynamical analysis connects GRU update gates with slow memory modes and other gates with Jacobian spectra ([Krishnamurthy et al., 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.00025)). Any benefit should therefore be framed as a selective-forgetting versus retention tradeoff, requiring empirical validation.
